section_1.title: From One to Many: The PDE Intuition
section_1.content: Transition from Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) to Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Explain that while ODEs track change over one variable (usually time), PDEs track change across multiple variables simultaneously (like time and position).
section_1.example: Visualize a single thermometer tracking a room's temperature (ODE) versus a high-tech 3D thermal grid showing how heat flows from a fireplace to the corners of the room (PDE).

section_2.title: Prerequisite Kit: The Partial Derivative
section_2.content: A quick visual refresher on partial derivatives (∂u/∂x). Explain the concept of 'holding one variable constant' while measuring the slope of another to ensure a smooth transition into complex equations.
section_2.example: A hiker (character) standing on a 3D mountain. Moving East-West represents the derivative with respect to 'x', while moving North-South represents 'y'. The PDE describes the shape of the entire mountain.

section_3.title: The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion
section_3.content: Introduce the Parabolic PDE (Heat Equation). Explain how the rate of change in time (∂u/∂t) is proportional to the 'curvature' of the temperature in space (∂²u/∂x²).
section_3.example: A Penguin sitting on a block of ice. An animation shows the 'heat profile' flattening out over time, moving from the warm penguin into the cold ice until the temperature curve becomes a straight line.

section_4.title: The Wave Equation: Modeling Vibration
section_4.content: Introduce the Hyperbolic PDE (Wave Equation). Discuss how the acceleration of a point (second derivative in time) is tied to its spatial tension (second derivative in space).
section_4.example: A guitar string plucked by a cat. The animation highlights a single point on the string oscillating up and down while the wave pulse travels horizontally, demonstrating the relationship between spatial shape and temporal motion.

section_5.title: The Big Three: Classification of PDEs
section_5.content: Briefly classify PDEs into three types based on their behavior: Elliptic (steady-state/equilibrium), Parabolic (diffusion), and Hyperbolic (waves/vibration).
section_5.example: A 'Water' themed graphic: A still, calm lake surface (Elliptic), ink drop spreading in the water (Parabolic), and a boat's wake moving across the surface (Hyperbolic).

section_6.title: The 'Walls' of the Math: Boundary Conditions
section_6.content: Explain that PDEs are 'wild' and need constraints to be solved. Introduce Dirichlet (fixed values) and Neumann (fixed flux/slope) boundary conditions.
section_6.example: A digital artist (character) using a 'clamping' tool. If the ends of a vibrating string are nailed down (Dirichlet), the wave looks different than if the ends are sliding on frictionless poles (Neumann).

section_7.title: Conclusion: The Language of the Universe
section_7.content: Summarize how PDEs are used in modern technology, from weather forecasting to designing airplane wings and simulating black holes.
section_7.example: A montage showing a smartphone, a SpaceX rocket, and a medical MRI machine—all devices that rely on solving PDEs to function correctly.

section_1.title: From One to Many: The PDE Intuition
section_1.content: Transition from Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) to Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Explain that while ODEs track change over one variable (usually time), PDEs track change across multiple variables simultaneously (like time and position).
section_1.example: Visualize a single thermometer tracking a room's temperature (ODE) versus a high-tech 3D thermal grid showing how heat flows from a fireplace to the corners of the room (PDE).

section_2.title: Prerequisite Kit: The Partial Derivative
section_2.content: A quick visual refresher on partial derivatives (∂u/∂x). Explain the concept of 'holding one variable constant' while measuring the slope of another to ensure a smooth transition into complex equations.
section_2.example: A hiker (character) standing on a 3D mountain. Moving East-West represents the derivative with respect to 'x', while moving North-South represents 'y'. The PDE describes the shape of the entire mountain.

section_3.title: The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion
section_3.content: Introduce the Parabolic PDE (Heat Equation). Explain how the rate of change in time (∂u/∂t) is proportional to the 'curvature' of the temperature in space (∂²u/∂x²).
section_3.example: A Penguin sitting on a block of ice. An animation shows the 'heat profile' flattening out over time, moving from the warm penguin into the cold ice until the temperature curve becomes a straight line.

section_4.title: The Wave Equation: Modeling Vibration
section_4.content: Introduce the Hyperbolic PDE (Wave Equation). Discuss how the acceleration of a point (second derivative in time) is tied to its spatial tension (second derivative in space).
section_4.example: A guitar string plucked by a cat. The animation highlights a single point on the string oscillating up and down while the wave pulse travels horizontally, demonstrating the relationship between spatial shape and temporal motion.

section_5.title: The Big Three: Classification of PDEs
section_5.content: Briefly classify PDEs into three types based on their behavior: Elliptic (steady-state/equilibrium), Parabolic (diffusion), and Hyperbolic (waves/vibration).
section_5.example: A 'Water' themed graphic: A still, calm lake surface (Elliptic), ink drop spreading in the water (Parabolic), and a boat's wake moving across the surface (Hyperbolic).

section_6.title: The 'Walls' of the Math: Boundary Conditions
section_6.content: Explain that PDEs are 'wild' and need constraints to be solved. Introduce Dirichlet (fixed values) and Neumann (fixed flux/slope) boundary conditions.
section_6.example: A digital artist (character) using a 'clamping' tool. If the ends of a vibrating string are nailed down (Dirichlet), the wave looks different than if the ends are sliding on frictionless poles (Neumann).

section_7.title: Conclusion: The Language of the Universe
section_7.content: Summarize how PDEs are used in modern technology, from weather forecasting to designing airplane wings and simulating black holes.
section_7.example: A montage showing a smartphone, a SpaceX rocket, and a medical MRI machine—all devices that rely on solving PDEs to function correctly.

section_1.title: From One to Many: The PDE Intuition
lecture_lines: ODEs track changes over one variable, like time.
But reality often involves multiple variables, like position.
PDEs describe how systems evolve in space and time.
animations: Draw a vertical rectangle (#FF0000) representing a thermometer. Label horizontal axis 't' (#FFFFFF).
Transform the rectangle into a 2D grid of small squares (#FFFFFF) to represent space.
Color central squares red (#FF0000) and outer squares blue (#0000FF). Animate heat spreading.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Kit: The Partial Derivative
lecture_lines: Partial derivatives measure change while holding other variables constant.
Imagine hiking a mountain along a single compass direction.
We isolate one dimension to understand complex multidimensional shapes.
animations: Draw a 3D wireframe mesh (#666666). Place a small yellow sphere (#FFFF00) on the surface.
Draw a green tangent line (#00FF00) along the x-direction through the sphere.
Draw a cyan tangent line (#00FFFF) along the y-direction through the sphere.

section_3.title: The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion
lecture_lines: The heat equation describes how temperature spreads through space.
Time change depends on the curvature of spatial temperature.
High curvature means heat flows quickly into colder regions.
Over time, temperature gradients flatten toward a steady state.
This parabolic behavior models diffusion in many physical systems.
animations: Show a blue rectangle (#0000FF) with an orange circle (#FFA500) labeled 'Heat Source'.
Display formula: d u / d t = alpha * d2 u / d x2. Highlight d u / d t in yellow (#FFFF00).
Plot a sharp red bell curve (#FF0000) over the blue rectangle.
Draw white arrows (#FFFFFF) pointing from the peak outward.
Animate the bell curve (#FF0000) flattening into a horizontal line.

section_4.title: The Wave Equation: Modeling Vibration
lecture_lines: The wave equation models oscillations like a plucked string.
Acceleration at a point depends on local spatial tension.
This creates disturbances that propagate as traveling waves.
Energy moves through the medium without displacing the matter.
Hyperbolic equations describe this dynamic, time-dependent behavior.
animations: Show a horizontal line (#FFFFFF). Display wave equation formula in white.
Animate a brown arc (#A52A2A) pulling and releasing the line center.
Highlight a single yellow dot (#FFFF00) on the line moving up and down.
Animate a cyan sine pulse (#00FFFF) traveling from left to right.
Add green vectors (#00FF00) showing curvature at the wave peak.

section_5.title: The Big Three: Classification of PDEs
lecture_lines: PDEs fall into three main types based on behavior.
Elliptic equations describe steady-state systems and equilibrium.
Parabolic equations model diffusion and spreading over time.
Hyperbolic equations represent waves and transport phenomena.
This classification helps us choose the right solving strategy.
animations: Display 'PDE Classification' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
Show 'Elliptic: Equilibrium' (#00FF00) next to a static smooth surface.
Show 'Parabolic: Diffusion' (#FFFF00) with a spreading Gaussian curve.
Show 'Hyperbolic: Waves' (#00FFFF) with two pulses moving in opposite directions.
Display 'Fundamental Physics' (#FFFFFF) below the three examples.

section_6.title: The 'Walls' of the Math: Boundary Conditions
lecture_lines: Boundaries define the physical limits of our PDE system.
Dirichlet conditions fix the value at the boundary's edge.
Neumann conditions specify the slope or flux across boundaries.
animations: Draw a horizontal white segment (#FFFFFF) with red circles (#FF0000) at endpoints.
Label the endpoints 'Dirichlet: Fixed Value' (#FF0000).
Replace circles with green tangent lines (#00FF00). Label 'Neumann: Fixed Slope'.

section_7.title: Conclusion: The Language of the Universe
lecture_lines: PDEs power weather forecasts and modern engineering designs.
They are the mathematical foundation for describing physical reality.
Mastering them unlocks the secrets of a changing world.
animations: Show icons: Smartphone (#FFFFFF), Rocket (#C0C0C0), and MRI (#A9A9A9).
Overlay yellow PDE formulas (#FFFF00) across the icons.
Display 'PDEs: The Language of the Universe' (#FFFFFF) centered.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        lines = [

            "Time change depends on the curvature of spatial temperature.",

        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        self.place_in_area(ice_block, "B2", "E5")

        self.lecture[1].set_color(FORMULA_HIGHLIGHT)

            y_range=[0, 1.5],

            y_length=2.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "include_ticks": False}
        ).move_to(ice_block.get_center())
        
        def bell_curve_func(x, sigma):
            return np.exp(-(x**2) / (2 * sigma**2))

        sigma_tracker = ValueTracker(0.3)

        self.play(GrowArrow(arrow_left), GrowArrow(arrow_right))
        self.wait(0.5)
        
        # Flattening animation
        self.play(
            sigma_tracker.animate.set_value(2.0),
            FadeOut(arrow_left),
            FadeOut(arrow_right),
            run_time=3
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # This parabolic behavior models diffusion in many physical systems.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # Final flattening to almost horizontal
        self.play(sigma_tracker.animate.set_value(10.0), run_time=2)
        self.wait(2)

            "ODEs track changes over one variable, like time.",
            "But reality often involves multiple variables, like position.",
            "PDEs describe how systems evolve in space and time."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("From One to Many: The PDE Intuition", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Draw a vertical rectangle (#FF0000) representing a thermometer. Label horizontal axis 't' (#FFFFFF).
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)

        self.place_at_grid(t_label, "F5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(thermometer), Create(t_axis), Write(t_label))
        self.wait(2)

        # Transform the rectangle into a 2D grid of small squares (#FFFFFF) to represent space.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        grid_rows, grid_cols = 5, 5
        grid_squares = VGroup(*[
            Square(side_length=0.4, color="#FFFFFF", stroke_width=2)

        ]).arrange_in_grid(rows=grid_rows, cols=grid_cols, buff=0.05)
        
        self.place_in_area(grid_squares, "B2", "E5")
        
        space_label = MathTex("x, y", color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(space_label, "F3", scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(
            Transform(thermometer, grid_squares),
            FadeOut(t_axis),
            Transform(t_label, space_label)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color central squares red (#FF0000) and outer squares blue (#0000FF). Animate heat spreading.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Use the transformed thermometer which is now visually a grid
        # We'll create a new set of squares for the colored version to avoid transform artifacts
        colored_grid = grid_squares.copy()
        
        def get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, heat_factor):
            # heat_factor goes from 0 to 1
            # intensity = 1 (red) at center, 0 (blue) at edges
            normalized_dist = dist / max_dist
            intensity = np.clip(1.0 - normalized_dist + (heat_factor * 0.8) - 0.2, 0, 1)
            return interpolate_color(BLUE, RED, intensity)

        # Initial colors
        max_dist = 3.0
        for i in range(grid_rows):
            for j in range(grid_cols):
                dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                idx = i * grid_cols + j
                colored_grid[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, 0), opacity=0.8)

        self.play(FadeIn(colored_grid), FadeOut(thermometer))
        
        heat_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def update_grid(obj):
            h = heat_tracker.get_value()
            for i in range(grid_rows):
                for j in range(grid_cols):
                    dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                    idx = i * grid_cols + j
                    obj[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, h), opacity=0.8)

        colored_grid.add_updater(update_grid)
        self.play(heat_tracker.animate.set_value(1), run_time=4)
        colored_grid.remove_updater(update_grid)
        
        self.wait(3)

    def construct(self):

            "ODEs track changes over one variable, like time.",
            "But reality often involves multiple variables, like position.",
            "PDEs describe how systems evolve in space and time."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("From One to Many: The PDE Intuition", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Draw a vertical rectangle (#FF0000) representing a thermometer. Label horizontal axis 't' (#FFFFFF).
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        thermometer = Rectangle(height=3, width=0.6, color="#FF0000", fill_opacity=0.8)

        ]).arrange_in_grid(rows=grid_rows, cols=grid_cols, buff=0.05)

        self.place_at_grid(space_label, "F3", scale_factor=0.8)

            FadeOut(t_axis),
            Transform(t_label, space_label)
        )

        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Use the transformed thermometer which is now visually a grid
        # We'll create a new set of squares for the colored version to avoid transform artifacts
        colored_grid = grid_squares.copy()
        
        def get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, heat_factor):
            # heat_factor goes from 0 to 1
            # intensity = 1 (red) at center, 0 (blue) at edges
            normalized_dist = dist / max_dist
            intensity = np.clip(1.0 - normalized_dist + (heat_factor * 0.8) - 0.2, 0, 1)
            return interpolate_color(BLUE, RED, intensity)

        # Initial colors
        max_dist = 3.0
        for i in range(grid_rows):
            for j in range(grid_cols):
                dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                idx = i * grid_cols + j
                colored_grid[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, 0), opacity=0.8)

        self.play(FadeIn(colored_grid), FadeOut(thermometer))
        
        heat_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def update_grid(obj):
            h = heat_tracker.get_value()
            for i in range(grid_rows):
                for j in range(grid_cols):
                    dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                    idx = i * grid_cols + j
                    obj[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, h), opacity=0.8)

        colored_grid.add_updater(update_grid)
        self.play(heat_tracker.animate.set_value(1), run_time=4)
        colored_grid.remove_updater(update_grid)
        
        self.wait(3)

    def construct(self):
        title = "The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion"
        lines = [
            "The heat equation describes how temperature spreads through space.",
            "Time change depends on the curvature of spatial temperature.",
            "High curvature means heat flows quickly into colder regions.",
            "Over time, temperature gradients flatten toward a steady state.",
            "This parabolic behavior models diffusion in many physical systems."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Colors
        RECT_COLOR = "#0000FF"
        SOURCE_COLOR = "#FFA500"
        FORMULA_HIGHLIGHT = "#FFFF00"
        CURVE_COLOR = "#FF0000"
        ARROW_COLOR = "#FFFFFF"

        self.lecture[0].set_color(RECT_COLOR)
        
        ice_block = Rectangle(width=4, height=3, color=RECT_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.3)
        self.place_in_area(ice_block, "B2", "E5")

        self.place_at_grid(heat_source, "C3")
        
        source_label = Text("Heat Source", font_size=18, color=SOURCE_COLOR)
        source_label.next_to(heat_source, UP, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(ice_block), FadeIn(heat_source), Write(source_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

        self.lecture[1].set_color(FORMULA_HIGHLIGHT)
        
        formula = MathTex(

            font_size=36
        )
        formula[0].set_color(FORMULA_HIGHLIGHT)
        self.place_in_area(formula, "A2", "A5")
        
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Plot a sharp red bell curve over the blue rectangle.
        self.lecture[2].set_color(CURVE_COLOR)
        
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-2, 2],
            y_range=[0, 1.5],
            x_length=4,
            y_length=2.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "include_ticks": False}
        ).move_to(ice_block.get_center())
        
        def bell_curve_func(x, sigma):
            return np.exp(-(x**2) / (2 * sigma**2))

        sigma_tracker = ValueTracker(0.3)
        curve = always_redraw(lambda: axes.plot(
            lambda x: bell_curve_func(x, sigma_tracker.get_value()),
            color=CURVE_COLOR
        ))
        
        self.play(Create(curve))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Draw white arrows pointing from the peak outward.
        # Animate the bell curve flattening.
        self.lecture[3].set_color(ARROW_COLOR)
        
        arrow_left = Arrow(start=axes.c2p(0, 1), end=axes.c2p(-1, 0.5), color=ARROW_COLOR, buff=0.1)
        arrow_right = Arrow(start=axes.c2p(0, 1), end=axes.c2p(1, 0.5), color=ARROW_COLOR, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(GrowArrow(arrow_left), GrowArrow(arrow_right))
        self.wait(0.5)
        
        # Flattening animation
        self.play(
            sigma_tracker.animate.set_value(2.0),
            FadeOut(arrow_left),
            FadeOut(arrow_right),
            run_time=3
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # This parabolic behavior models diffusion in many physical systems.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # Final flattening to almost horizontal
        self.play(sigma_tracker.animate.set_value(10.0), run_time=2)
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title = "The Wave Equation: Modeling Vibration"
        lines = [
            "The wave equation models oscillations like a plucked string.",
            "Acceleration at a point depends on local spatial tension.",
            "This creates disturbances that propagate as traveling waves.",
            "Energy moves through the medium without displacing the matter.",
            "Hyperbolic equations describe this dynamic, time-dependent behavior."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Helper for wave pulse
        def pulse_func(x, t, center=3.0, width=0.5, amp=0.5):
            # Traveling pulse f(x - ct)
            c = 1.5
            pos = center + c * t
            # Ensure it wraps or just disappears
            if pos > 6.0: pos = 0.0 + (pos - 6.0)
            return amp * np.exp(-((x - pos) ** 2) / (2 * width ** 2))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Horizontal string
        string = Line(self.grid["D1"], self.grid["D6"], color="#FFFFFF")
        # Formula: d^2u/dt^2 = c^2 d^2u/dx^2
        formula = MathTex(r"\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(string), Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Brown arc pulling the string
        # We'll represent the pulling by distorting the string
        arc = ArcBetweenPoints(self.grid["C3"] + LEFT*0.2, self.grid["C3"] + RIGHT*0.2, angle=TAU/4, color="#A52A2A")
        
        pulled_string = VMobject(color="#FFFFFF")
        pulled_string.set_points_as_corners([
            self.grid["D1"],
            self.grid["D2"],
            self.grid["C3"], # Pulled up
            self.grid["D4"],
            self.grid["D5"],
            self.grid["D6"]
        ]).make_smooth()

        self.play(Create(arc))
        self.play(Transform(string, pulled_string))
        self.wait(1)
        self.play(FadeOut(arc), string.animate.set_points_as_corners([self.grid["D1"], self.grid["D6"]]))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Traveling pulse
        time_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def get_wave_path():
            points = []
            start_x = self.grid["D1"][0]
            end_x = self.grid["D6"][0]
            y_base = self.grid["D1"][1]
            for x in np.linspace(start_x, end_x, 50):
                # Map relative x to center 3.0
                rel_x = (x - start_x) / (end_x - start_x) * 6.0 
                y_offset = pulse_func(rel_x, time_tracker.get_value())
                points.append([x, y_base + y_offset, 0])
            return points

        wave_line = VMobject(color="#00FFFF")
        wave_line.set_points_as_corners(get_wave_path())
        wave_line.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_points_as_corners(get_wave_path()))
        
        # Yellow dot on the line at x=3.5 (Grid D4-ish)
        dot_x_coord = self.grid["D4"][0]
        dot_rel_x = (dot_x_coord - self.grid["D1"][0]) / (self.grid["D6"][0] - self.grid["D1"][0]) * 6.0
        
        dot = Dot(color="#FFFF00")
        dot.add_updater(lambda m: m.move_to([
            dot_x_coord, 
            self.grid["D1"][1] + pulse_func(dot_rel_x, time_tracker.get_value()), 
            0
        ]))

        self.play(FadeOut(string), Create(wave_line), FadeIn(dot))
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(4), run_time=4, rate_func=linear)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[3].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Energy moving pulse (already happening), emphasizing the dot stays at same X
        # Add a vertical dashed line to show the dot only moves up/down
        v_line = DashedLine(self.grid["C4"], self.grid["E4"], color=GRAY, stroke_opacity=0.5)
        self.add(v_line)
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(8), run_time=4, rate_func=linear)
        self.remove(v_line)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[4].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Green vectors showing curvature at peak
        # We find where the pulse center is currently
        def get_peak_pos():
            t = time_tracker.get_value()
            c = 1.5
            center = 3.0
            pos_rel = (center + c * t) % 6.0
            x_coord = self.grid["D1"][0] + (pos_rel / 6.0) * (self.grid["D6"][0] - self.grid["D1"][0])
            y_coord = self.grid["D1"][1] + 0.5 # Amp
            return [x_coord, y_coord, 0]

        vector_up = Arrow(start=ORIGIN, end=UP*0.5, color="#00FF00", buff=0)
        vector_up.add_updater(lambda m: m.move_to(get_peak_pos()))
        
        self.play(GrowArrow(vector_up))
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(12), run_time=4, rate_func=linear)
        
        self.wait(2)

    def construct(self):
        title_text = "The Big Three: Classification of PDEs"
        lecture_lines = [
            "PDEs fall into three main types based on behavior.",
            "Elliptic equations describe steady-state systems and equilibrium.",
            "Parabolic equations model diffusion and spreading over time.",
            "Hyperbolic equations represent waves and transport phenomena.",
            "This classification helps us choose the right solving strategy."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # PDEs fall into three main types based on behavior.
        # Display 'PDE Classification' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        pde_class_label = Text("PDE Classification", font_size=32, color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(pde_class_label, "A2", "A5")
        self.play(Write(pde_class_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # Show 'Elliptic: Equilibrium' (#00FF00) next to a static smooth surface.

        self.place_at_grid(elliptic_label, "B2", scale_factor=0.8)

        self.place_at_grid(elliptic_surface, "B4", scale_factor=1.0)

        curve_pos = self.grid["C4"]

        def get_gaussian_points(sigma):
            return ParametricFunction(
                lambda t: np.array([t, 0.4 * (1/sigma) * np.exp(-t**2 / (2 * sigma**2)), 0]),
                t_range=[-1.5, 1.5]
            ).scale(0.6).move_to(curve_pos).get_points()

        parabolic_curve = ParametricFunction(
            lambda t: np.array([t, 0.4 * (1/0.2) * np.exp(-t**2 / (2 * 0.2**2)), 0]),
            t_range=[-1.5, 1.5],
            color="#FFFF00"
        ).scale(0.6).move_to(curve_pos)
        
        # Update curve points in-place to optimize performance
        parabolic_curve.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_points(get_gaussian_points(sigma_tracker.get_value())))
        
        self.play(FadeIn(parabolic_label), Create(parabolic_curve))

        pulse2 = ParametricFunction(lambda t: [t, pulse_func(t), 0], t_range=[-0.5, 0.5], color="#00FFFF")

        self.place_at_grid(pulse2, "D4", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(hyperbolic_label), Create(pulse1), Create(pulse2))
        self.play(

section_1.title: From One to Many: The PDE Intuition
section_1.content: Transition from Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) to Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Explain that while ODEs track change over one variable (usually time), PDEs track change across multiple variables simultaneously (like time and position).
section_1.example: Visualize a single thermometer tracking a room's temperature (ODE) versus a high-tech 3D thermal grid showing how heat flows from a fireplace to the corners of the room (PDE).

section_2.title: Prerequisite Kit: The Partial Derivative
section_2.content: A quick visual refresher on partial derivatives (∂u/∂x). Explain the concept of 'holding one variable constant' while measuring the slope of another to ensure a smooth transition into complex equations.
section_2.example: A hiker (character) standing on a 3D mountain. Moving East-West represents the derivative with respect to 'x', while moving North-South represents 'y'. The PDE describes the shape of the entire mountain.

section_3.title: The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion
section_3.content: Introduce the Parabolic PDE (Heat Equation). Explain how the rate of change in time (∂u/∂t) is proportional to the 'curvature' of the temperature in space (∂²u/∂x²).
section_3.example: A Penguin sitting on a block of ice. An animation shows the 'heat profile' flattening out over time, moving from the warm penguin into the cold ice until the temperature curve becomes a straight line.

section_4.title: The Wave Equation: Modeling Vibration
section_4.content: Introduce the Hyperbolic PDE (Wave Equation). Discuss how the acceleration of a point (second derivative in time) is tied to its spatial tension (second derivative in space).
section_4.example: A guitar string plucked by a cat. The animation highlights a single point on the string oscillating up and down while the wave pulse travels horizontally, demonstrating the relationship between spatial shape and temporal motion.

section_5.title: The Big Three: Classification of PDEs
section_5.content: Briefly classify PDEs into three types based on their behavior: Elliptic (steady-state/equilibrium), Parabolic (diffusion), and Hyperbolic (waves/vibration).
section_5.example: A 'Water' themed graphic: A still, calm lake surface (Elliptic), ink drop spreading in the water (Parabolic), and a boat's wake moving across the surface (Hyperbolic).

section_6.title: The 'Walls' of the Math: Boundary Conditions
section_6.content: Explain that PDEs are 'wild' and need constraints to be solved. Introduce Dirichlet (fixed values) and Neumann (fixed flux/slope) boundary conditions.
section_6.example: A digital artist (character) using a 'clamping' tool. If the ends of a vibrating string are nailed down (Dirichlet), the wave looks different than if the ends are sliding on frictionless poles (Neumann).

section_7.title: Conclusion: The Language of the Universe
section_7.content: Summarize how PDEs are used in modern technology, from weather forecasting to designing airplane wings and simulating black holes.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "ODEs track changes over one variable, like time.",
            "But reality often involves multiple variables, like position.",
            "PDEs describe how systems evolve in space and time."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("From One to Many: The PDE Intuition", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Draw a vertical rectangle (#FF0000) representing a thermometer. Label horizontal axis 't' (#FFFFFF).
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        thermometer = Rectangle(height=3, width=0.6, color="#FF0000", fill_opacity=0.8)
        self.place_in_area(thermometer, "B3", "E3")
        
        t_axis = Line(start=self.grid["F2"], end=self.grid["F4"], color=WHITE)
        t_label = MathTex("t", color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(t_label, "F5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(thermometer), Create(t_axis), Write(t_label))
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Transform the rectangle into a 2D grid of small squares (#FFFFFF) to represent space.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        grid_rows, grid_cols = 5, 5
        grid_squares = VGroup(*[
            Square(side_length=0.4, color="#FFFFFF", stroke_width=2)
            for _ in range(grid_rows * grid_cols)
        ]).arrange_in_grid(rows=grid_rows, cols=grid_cols, buff=0.05)
        
        self.place_in_area(grid_squares, "B2", "E5")
        
        space_label = MathTex("x, y", color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(space_label, "F3", scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(
            Transform(thermometer, grid_squares),
            FadeOut(t_axis),
            Transform(t_label, space_label)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color central squares red (#FF0000) and outer squares blue (#0000FF). Animate heat spreading.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Use the transformed thermometer which is now visually a grid
        # We'll create a new set of squares for the colored version to avoid transform artifacts
        colored_grid = grid_squares.copy()
        
        def get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, heat_factor):
            # heat_factor goes from 0 to 1
            # intensity = 1 (red) at center, 0 (blue) at edges
            normalized_dist = dist / max_dist
            intensity = np.clip(1.0 - normalized_dist + (heat_factor * 0.8) - 0.2, 0, 1)
            return interpolate_color(BLUE, RED, intensity)

        # Initial colors
        max_dist = 3.0
        for i in range(grid_rows):
            for j in range(grid_cols):
                dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                idx = i * grid_cols + j
                colored_grid[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, 0), opacity=0.8)

        self.play(FadeIn(colored_grid), FadeOut(thermometer))
        
        heat_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def update_grid(obj):
            h = heat_tracker.get_value()
            for i in range(grid_rows):
                for j in range(grid_cols):
                    dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                    idx = i * grid_cols + j
                    obj[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, h), opacity=0.8)

        colored_grid.add_updater(update_grid)
        self.play(heat_tracker.animate.set_value(1), run_time=4)
        colored_grid.remove_updater(update_grid)
        
        self.wait(3)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title = "The Wave Equation: Modeling Vibration"
        lines = [
            "The wave equation models oscillations like a plucked string.",
            "Acceleration at a point depends on local spatial tension.",
            "This creates disturbances that propagate as traveling waves.",
            "Energy moves through the medium without displacing the matter.",
            "Hyperbolic equations describe this dynamic, time-dependent behavior."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Helper for wave pulse
        def pulse_func(x, t, center=3.0, width=0.5, amp=0.5):
            # Traveling pulse f(x - ct)
            c = 1.5
            pos = center + c * t
            # Simple wrapping for continuous movement in demo
            pos = (pos % 7.0) - 0.5 
            return amp * np.exp(-((x - pos) ** 2) / (2 * width ** 2))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Horizontal string
        string = Line(self.grid["D1"], self.grid["D6"], color="#FFFFFF")
        # Formula: d^2u/dt^2 = c^2 d^2u/dx^2
        formula = MathTex(r"\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(string), Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Brown arc pulling the string
        arc = ArcBetweenPoints(self.grid["C3"] + LEFT*0.2, self.grid["C3"] + RIGHT*0.2, angle=TAU/4, color="#A52A2A")
        
        pulled_string = VMobject(color="#FFFFFF")
        pulled_string.set_points_as_corners([
            self.grid["D1"],
            self.grid["D2"],
            self.grid["C3"], # Pulled up point
            self.grid["D4"],
            self.grid["D5"],
            self.grid["D6"]
        ]).make_smooth()

        self.play(Create(arc))
        self.play(Transform(string, pulled_string))
        self.wait(1)
        self.play(FadeOut(arc), string.animate.set_points_as_corners([self.grid["D1"], self.grid["D6"]]))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Traveling pulse simulation
        time_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def get_wave_path():
            points = []
            start_x = self.grid["D1"][0]
            end_x = self.grid["D6"][0]
            y_base = self.grid["D1"][1]
            # Sample 50 points across the string segment
            for x in np.linspace(start_x, end_x, 50):
                # Map physical x to internal relative coordinate (0-6)
                rel_x = (x - start_x) / (end_x - start_x) * 6.0 
                y_offset = pulse_func(rel_x, time_tracker.get_value())
                points.append([x, y_base + y_offset, 0])
            return points

        wave_line = VMobject(color="#00FFFF")
        wave_line.set_points_as_corners(get_wave_path())
        wave_line.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_points_as_corners(get_wave_path()))
        
        # Yellow dot on the string at x=3.5 (near Grid D4)
        dot_x_coord = self.grid["D4"][0]
        dot_rel_x = (dot_x_coord - self.grid["D1"][0]) / (self.grid["D6"][0] - self.grid["D1"][0]) * 6.0
        
        dot = Dot(color="#FFFF00")
        dot.add_updater(lambda m: m.move_to([
            dot_x_coord, 
            self.grid["D1"][1] + pulse_func(dot_rel_x, time_tracker.get_value()), 
            0
        ]))

        self.play(FadeOut(string), Create(wave_line), FadeIn(dot))
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(4), run_time=4, rate_func=linear)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[3].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Add vertical guide to show the dot stays on its X-axis
        v_line = DashedLine(self.grid["C4"], self.grid["E4"], color=GRAY, stroke_opacity=0.3)
        self.add(v_line)
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(8), run_time=4, rate_func=linear)
        self.remove(v_line)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[4].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Green vectors showing displacement/tension at wave peak
        def get_peak_pos():
            t = time_tracker.get_value()
            c = 1.5
            center = 3.0
            pos_rel = ((center + c * t) % 7.0) - 0.5
            x_coord = self.grid["D1"][0] + (pos_rel / 6.0) * (self.grid["D6"][0] - self.grid["D1"][0])
            # Clamp to string bounds for visual consistency
            x_coord = np.clip(x_coord, self.grid["D1"][0], self.grid["D6"][0])
            y_coord = self.grid["D1"][1] + pulse_func(pos_rel, t)
            return [x_coord, y_coord, 0]

        peak_vector = Arrow(start=DOWN*0.3, end=UP*0.3, color="#00FF00", buff=0)
        peak_vector.add_updater(lambda m: m.move_to(get_peak_pos()))
        
        self.play(GrowArrow(peak_vector))
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(12), run_time=4, rate_func=linear)
        
        self.wait(2)

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)

        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title_text = "The Big Three: Classification of PDEs"
        lecture_lines = [
            "PDEs fall into three main types based on behavior.",
            "Elliptic equations describe steady-state systems and equilibrium.",
            "Parabolic equations model diffusion and spreading over time.",
            "Hyperbolic equations represent waves and transport phenomena.",
            "This classification helps us choose the right solving strategy."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # PDEs fall into three main types based on behavior.
        # Display 'PDE Classification' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        pde_class_label = Text("PDE Classification", font_size=32, color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(pde_class_label, "A2", "A5")
        self.play(Write(pde_class_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Elliptic equations describe steady-state systems and equilibrium.
        # Show 'Elliptic: Equilibrium' (#00FF00) next to a static smooth surface.
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00FF00")
        elliptic_label = Text("Elliptic: Equilibrium", font_size=20, color="#00FF00")
        self.place_at_grid(elliptic_label, "B2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        elliptic_surface = Line(LEFT, RIGHT, color="#00FF00")
        self.place_at_grid(elliptic_surface, "B4", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(elliptic_label), Create(elliptic_surface))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Parabolic equations model diffusion and spreading over time.
        # Show 'Parabolic: Diffusion' (#FFFF00) with a spreading Gaussian curve.
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFF00")
        parabolic_label = Text("Parabolic: Diffusion", font_size=20, color="#FFFF00")
        self.place_at_grid(parabolic_label, "C2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        sigma_tracker = ValueTracker(0.2)
        curve_pos = self.grid["C4"]
        
        # Helper to get Gaussian points
        def get_gaussian_points(sigma):
            return ParametricFunction(
                lambda t: np.array([t, 0.4 * (1/sigma) * np.exp(-t**2 / (2 * sigma**2)), 0]),
                t_range=[-1.5, 1.5]
            ).scale(0.6).move_to(curve_pos).get_points()

        parabolic_curve = ParametricFunction(
            lambda t: np.array([t, 0.4 * (1/0.2) * np.exp(-t**2 / (2 * 0.2**2)), 0]),
            t_range=[-1.5, 1.5],
            color="#FFFF00"
        ).scale(0.6).move_to(curve_pos)
        
        # Update curve points in-place to optimize performance
        parabolic_curve.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_points(get_gaussian_points(sigma_tracker.get_value())))
        
        self.play(FadeIn(parabolic_label), Create(parabolic_curve))
        self.play(sigma_tracker.animate.set_value(1.2), run_time=2)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Hyperbolic equations represent waves and transport phenomena.
        # Show 'Hyperbolic: Waves' (#00FFFF) with two pulses moving in opposite directions.
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#00FFFF")
        hyperbolic_label = Text("Hyperbolic: Waves", font_size=20, color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(hyperbolic_label, "D2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        pulse_func = lambda x: 0.4 * np.exp(-x**2 / 0.05)
        pulse1 = ParametricFunction(lambda t: [t, pulse_func(t), 0], t_range=[-0.5, 0.5], color="#00FFFF")
        pulse2 = ParametricFunction(lambda t: [t, pulse_func(t), 0], t_range=[-0.5, 0.5], color="#00FFFF")
        
        self.place_at_grid(pulse1, "D4", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(pulse2, "D4", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(hyperbolic_label), Create(pulse1), Create(pulse2))
        self.play(
            pulse1.animate.shift(LEFT * 1.2),
            pulse2.animate.shift(RIGHT * 1.2),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # This classification helps us choose the right solving strategy.
        # Display 'Fundamental Physics' (#FFFFFF) below the three examples.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)
        fundamental_physics = Text("Fundamental Physics", font_size=28, color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(fundamental_physics, "F2", "F5")
        
        self.play(Write(fundamental_physics))
        self.wait(2)

outline.title: Prerequisite Kit: The Partial Derivative
outline.content: A quick visual refresher on partial derivatives (∂u/∂x). Explain the concept of 'holding one variable constant' while measuring the slope of another to ensure a smooth transition into complex equations.
outline.example: A hiker (character) standing on a 3D mountain. Moving East-West represents the derivative with respect to 'x', while moving North-South represents 'y'. The PDE describes the shape of the entire mountain.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Data from storyboard
        title = "Prerequisite Kit: The Partial Derivative"
        lines = [
            "- Partial derivatives measure change while holding other variables constant.",
            "- Imagine hiking a mountain along a single compass direction.",
            "- We isolate one dimension to understand complex multidimensional shapes."
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Load mountain SVG [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/mountain.svg]
        # We use the SVG to represent the mountain surface
        try:
            mountain = SVGMobject("/scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/mountain.svg")
        except Exception:
            # Fallback if file not found during local dev (not expected in MAS)
            mountain = Triangle().scale(2)
            
        mountain.set_color("#666666")
        self.place_in_area(mountain, 'A1', 'F6', scale_factor=1.8)
        
        # Small yellow sphere (#FFFF00) representing the hiker
        sphere = Dot(color="#FFFF00", radius=0.1)
        # Place sphere at a visual 'slope' location relative to the mountain center
        self.place_at_grid(sphere, 'C3')
        
        # Highlight first lecture line in Yellow (matching sphere)
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.play(
            DrawBorderThenFill(mountain, run_time=2),
            FadeIn(sphere, shift=UP)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Green tangent line (#00FF00) along the x-direction (horizontal-ish)
        tangent_x = Line(
            start=sphere.get_center() + LEFT * 1.0 + DOWN * 0.1,
            end=sphere.get_center() + RIGHT * 1.0 + UP * 0.1,
            color="#00FF00",
            stroke_width=6
        )
        
        # Highlight second lecture line in Green (matching tangent line)
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(GREEN)
        self.play(Create(tangent_x))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Cyan tangent line (#00FFFF) along the y-direction (slanted-ish)
        tangent_y = Line(
            start=sphere.get_center() + LEFT * 0.4 + UP * 0.8,
            end=sphere.get_center() + RIGHT * 0.4 + DOWN * 0.8,
            color="#00FFFF",
            stroke_width=6
        )
        
        # Highlight third lecture line in Cyan (matching tangent line)
        # Using hex code "#00FFFF" to avoid NameError for 'CYAN' constant
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        self.play(Create(tangent_y))
        self.wait(2)

outline.title: The 'Walls' of the Math: Boundary Conditions
outline.content: Explain that PDEs are 'wild' and need constraints to be solved. Introduce Dirichlet (fixed values) and Neumann (fixed flux/slope) boundary conditions.
outline.example: A digital artist (character) using a 'clamping' tool. If the ends of a vibrating string are nailed down (Dirichlet), the wave looks different than if the ends are sliding on frictionless poles (Neumann).

storyboard.title: The 'Walls' of the Math: Boundary Conditions
lecture_lines: Boundaries define the physical limits of our PDE system.
Dirichlet conditions fix the value at the boundary's edge.
Neumann conditions specify the slope or flux across boundaries.
animations: Draw a horizontal white segment (#FFFFFF) with red circles (#FF0000) at endpoints.
Label the endpoints 'Dirichlet: Fixed Value' (#FF0000).
Replace circles with green tangent lines (#00FF00). Label 'Neumann: Fixed Slope'.

outline.title: From One to Many: The PDE Intuition
outline.content: Transition from Ordinary Differential Equations (ODEs) to Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Explain that while ODEs track change over one variable (usually time), PDEs track change across multiple variables simultaneously (like time and position).
outline.example: Visualize a single thermometer tracking a room's temperature (ODE) versus a high-tech 3D thermal grid showing how heat flows from a fireplace to the corners of the room (PDE).

storyboard.title: From One to Many: The PDE Intuition
lecture_lines: ODEs track changes over one variable, like time.
But reality often involves multiple variables, like position.
PDEs describe how systems evolve in space and time.

Transform the rectangle into a 2D grid of small squares (#FFFFFF) to represent space.

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "ODEs track changes over one variable, like time.",
            "But reality often involves multiple variables, like position.",
            "PDEs describe how systems evolve in space and time."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("From One to Many: The PDE Intuition", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Draw a vertical rectangle (#FF0000) representing a thermometer. Label horizontal axis 't' (#FFFFFF).
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        thermometer = Rectangle(height=3, width=0.6, color="#FF0000", fill_opacity=0.8)
        self.place_in_area(thermometer, "B3", "E3")
        
        t_axis = Line(start=self.grid["F2"], end=self.grid["F4"], color=WHITE)
        t_label = MathTex("t", color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(t_label, "F5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(thermometer), Create(t_axis), Write(t_label))
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Transform the rectangle into a 2D grid of small squares (#FFFFFF) to represent space.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        grid_rows, grid_cols = 5, 5
        grid_squares = VGroup(*[
            Square(side_length=0.4, color="#FFFFFF", stroke_width=2)
            for _ in range(grid_rows * grid_cols)
        ]).arrange_in_grid(rows=grid_rows, cols=grid_cols, buff=0.05)
        
        self.place_in_area(grid_squares, "B2", "E5")
        
        space_label = MathTex("x, y", color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(space_label, "F3", scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(
            Transform(thermometer, grid_squares),
            FadeOut(t_axis),
            Transform(t_label, space_label)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color central squares red (#FF0000) and outer squares blue (#0000FF). Animate heat spreading.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Use the transformed thermometer which is now visually a grid
        # We'll create a new set of squares for the colored version to avoid transform artifacts
        colored_grid = grid_squares.copy()
        
        def get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, heat_factor):
            # heat_factor goes from 0 to 1
            # intensity = 1 (red) at center, 0 (blue) at edges
            normalized_dist = dist / max_dist
            intensity = np.clip(1.0 - normalized_dist + (heat_factor * 0.8) - 0.2, 0, 1)
            return interpolate_color(BLUE, RED, intensity)

        # Initial colors
        max_dist = 3.0
        for i in range(grid_rows):
            for j in range(grid_cols):
                dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                idx = i * grid_cols + j
                colored_grid[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, 0), opacity=0.8)

        self.play(FadeIn(colored_grid), FadeOut(thermometer))
        
        heat_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def update_grid(obj):
            h = heat_tracker.get_value()
            for i in range(grid_rows):
                for j in range(grid_cols):
                    dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                    idx = i * grid_cols + j
                    obj[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, h), opacity=0.8)

        colored_grid.add_updater(update_grid)
        self.play(heat_tracker.animate.set_value(1), run_time=4)
        colored_grid.remove_updater(update_grid)
        
        self.wait(3)

outline.title: The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion
outline.content: Introduce the Parabolic PDE (Heat Equation). Explain how the rate of change in time (∂u/∂t) is proportional to the 'curvature' of the temperature in space (∂²u/∂x²).
outline.example: A Penguin sitting on a block of ice. An animation shows the 'heat profile' flattening out over time, moving from the warm penguin into the cold ice until the temperature curve becomes a straight line.

storyboard.title: The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion
lecture_lines: The heat equation describes how temperature spreads through space.
Time change depends on the curvature of spatial temperature.
High curvature means heat flows quickly into colder regions.
Over time, temperature gradients flatten toward a steady state.
This parabolic behavior models diffusion in many physical systems.
animations: Show a blue rectangle (#0000FF) with an orange circle (#FFA500) labeled 'Heat Source'.
Display formula: d u / d t = alpha * d2 u / d x2. Highlight d u / d t in yellow (#FFFF00).
Plot a sharp red bell curve (#FF0000) over the blue rectangle.
Draw white arrows (#FFFFFF) pointing from the peak outward.
Animate the bell curve (#FF0000) flattening into a horizontal line.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        elliptic_surface = Line(LEFT, RIGHT, color="#00FF00")

        self.play(FadeIn(elliptic_label), Create(elliptic_surface))

                t_range=[-1.5, 1.5]
            ).scale(0.6).move_to(curve_pos).get_points()

        parabolic_curve = ParametricFunction(

            t_range=[-1.5, 1.5],

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title = "The Wave Equation: Modeling Vibration"
        lines = [
            "The wave equation models oscillations like a plucked string.",
            "Acceleration at a point depends on local spatial tension.",
            "This creates disturbances that propagate as traveling waves.",
            "Energy moves through the medium without displacing the matter.",
            "Hyperbolic equations describe this dynamic, time-dependent behavior."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Helper for wave pulse
        def pulse_func(x, t, center=3.0, width=0.5, amp=0.5):
            # Traveling pulse f(x - ct)
            c = 1.5
            pos = center + c * t
            # Simple wrapping for continuous movement in demo
            pos = (pos % 7.0) - 0.5 
            return amp * np.exp(-((x - pos) ** 2) / (2 * width ** 2))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Horizontal string
        string = Line(self.grid["D1"], self.grid["D6"], color="#FFFFFF")
        # Formula: d^2u/dt^2 = c^2 d^2u/dx^2
        formula = MathTex(r"\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(string), Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Brown arc pulling the string
        arc = ArcBetweenPoints(self.grid["C3"] + LEFT*0.2, self.grid["C3"] + RIGHT*0.2, angle=TAU/4, color="#A52A2A")
        
        pulled_string = VMobject(color="#FFFFFF")
        pulled_string.set_points_as_corners([
            self.grid["D1"],
            self.grid["D2"],
            self.grid["C3"], # Pulled up point
            self.grid["D4"],
            self.grid["D5"],
            self.grid["D6"]
        ]).make_smooth()

        self.play(Create(arc))
        self.play(Transform(string, pulled_string))
        self.wait(1)
        self.play(FadeOut(arc), string.animate.set_points_as_corners([self.grid["D1"], self.grid["D6"]]))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Traveling pulse simulation
        time_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def get_wave_path():
            points = []
            start_x = self.grid["D1"][0]
            end_x = self.grid["D6"][0]
            y_base = self.grid["D1"][1]
            # Sample 50 points across the string segment
            for x in np.linspace(start_x, end_x, 50):
                # Map physical x to internal relative coordinate (0-6)
                rel_x = (x - start_x) / (end_x - start_x) * 6.0 
                y_offset = pulse_func(rel_x, time_tracker.get_value())
                points.append([x, y_base + y_offset, 0])
            return points

        wave_line = VMobject(color="#00FFFF")
        wave_line.set_points_as_corners(get_wave_path())
        wave_line.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_points_as_corners(get_wave_path()))
        
        # Yellow dot on the string at x=3.5 (near Grid D4)
        dot_x_coord = self.grid["D4"][0]
        dot_rel_x = (dot_x_coord - self.grid["D1"][0]) / (self.grid["D6"][0] - self.grid["D1"][0]) * 6.0
        
        dot = Dot(color="#FFFF00")
        dot.add_updater(lambda m: m.move_to([
            dot_x_coord, 
            self.grid["D1"][1] + pulse_func(dot_rel_x, time_tracker.get_value()), 
            0
        ]))

        self.play(FadeOut(string), Create(wave_line), FadeIn(dot))
        self.play(time_tracker.animate.set_value(4), run_time=4, rate_func=linear)

        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        lecture_lines = [

            "But reality often involves multiple variables, like position.",
            "PDEs describe how systems evolve in space and time."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("From One to Many: The PDE Intuition", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Draw a vertical rectangle (#FF0000) representing a thermometer. Label horizontal axis 't' (#FFFFFF).
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        thermometer = Rectangle(height=3, width=0.6, color="#FF0000", fill_opacity=0.8)
        self.place_in_area(thermometer, "B3", "E3")
        
        t_axis = Line(start=self.grid["F2"], end=self.grid["F4"], color=WHITE)
        t_label = MathTex("t", color="#FFFFFF")
        # Fix: Centering t_label under the thermometer column (Issue 25)
        self.place_at_grid(t_label, "F3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Create(thermometer), Create(t_axis), Write(t_label))
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Transform the rectangle into a 2D grid of small squares (#FFFFFF) to represent space.

        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        grid_rows, grid_cols = 5, 5
        grid_squares = VGroup(*[

            for _ in range(grid_rows * grid_cols)
        ]).arrange_in_grid(rows=grid_rows, cols=grid_cols, buff=0.05)
        
        self.place_in_area(grid_squares, "B2", "E5")
        
        space_label = MathTex("x, y", color="#FFFFFF")

            Transform(thermometer, grid_squares),
            FadeOut(t_axis),
            Transform(t_label, space_label)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)

        colored_grid = grid_squares.copy()

            # heat_factor goes from 0 to 1

            normalized_dist = dist / max_dist
            intensity = np.clip(1.0 - normalized_dist + (heat_factor * 0.8) - 0.2, 0, 1)
            return interpolate_color(BLUE, RED, intensity)

        # Initial colors
        max_dist = 3.0
        for i in range(grid_rows):
            for j in range(grid_cols):
                dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                idx = i * grid_cols + j
                colored_grid[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, 0), opacity=0.8)

        self.play(FadeIn(colored_grid), FadeOut(thermometer))
        
        heat_tracker = ValueTracker(0)
        
        def update_grid(obj):
            h = heat_tracker.get_value()
            for i in range(grid_rows):
                for j in range(grid_cols):
                    dist = np.sqrt((i - grid_rows//2)**2 + (j - grid_cols//2)**2)
                    idx = i * grid_cols + j
                    obj[idx].set_fill(get_color_for_dist(dist, max_dist, h), opacity=0.8)

        colored_grid.add_updater(update_grid)
        self.play(heat_tracker.animate.set_value(1), run_time=4)
        colored_grid.remove_updater(update_grid)
        
        self.wait(3)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title_text = "The Big Three: Classification of PDEs"
        lecture_lines = [
            "PDEs fall into three main types based on behavior.",
            "Elliptic equations describe steady-state systems and equilibrium.",
            "Parabolic equations model diffusion and spreading over time.",
            "Hyperbolic equations represent waves and transport phenomena.",
            "This classification helps us choose the right solving strategy."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # PDEs fall into three main types based on behavior.
        # Display 'PDE Classification' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        pde_class_label = Text("PDE Classification", font_size=32, color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(pde_class_label, "A2", "A5")
        self.play(Write(pde_class_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Elliptic equations describe steady-state systems and equilibrium.
        # Show 'Elliptic: Equilibrium' (#00FF00) next to a static smooth surface.
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00FF00")
        elliptic_label = Text("Elliptic: Equilibrium", font_size=20, color="#00FF00")
        self.place_at_grid(elliptic_label, "B3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        elliptic_surface = Line(LEFT, RIGHT, color="#00FF00")
        self.place_at_grid(elliptic_surface, "B4", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(elliptic_label), Create(elliptic_surface))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Parabolic equations model diffusion and spreading over time.
        # Show 'Parabolic: Diffusion' (#FFFF00) with a spreading Gaussian curve.
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFF00")
        parabolic_label = Text("Parabolic: Diffusion", font_size=20, color="#FFFF00")
        self.place_at_grid(parabolic_label, "C3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        sigma_tracker = ValueTracker(0.2)
        curve_pos = self.grid["C4"]
        
        # Helper to get Gaussian points
        def get_gaussian_points(sigma):
            return ParametricFunction(
                lambda t: np.array([t, 0.4 * (1/sigma) * np.exp(-t**2 / (2 * sigma**2)), 0]),
                t_range=[-1.5, 1.5]
            ).scale(0.6).move_to(curve_pos).get_points()

        parabolic_curve = ParametricFunction(
            lambda t: np.array([t, 0.4 * (1/0.2) * np.exp(-t**2 / (2 * 0.2**2)), 0]),
            t_range=[-1.5, 1.5],
            color="#FFFF00"
        ).scale(0.6).move_to(curve_pos)
        
        # Update curve points in-place to optimize performance
        parabolic_curve.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_points(get_gaussian_points(sigma_tracker.get_value())))
        
        self.play(FadeIn(parabolic_label), Create(parabolic_curve))
        self.play(sigma_tracker.animate.set_value(1.2), run_time=2)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Hyperbolic equations represent waves and transport phenomena.
        # Show 'Hyperbolic: Waves' (#00FFFF) with two pulses moving in opposite directions.
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#00FFFF")
        hyperbolic_label = Text("Hyperbolic: Waves", font_size=20, color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(hyperbolic_label, "D3", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        pulse_func = lambda x: 0.4 * np.exp(-x**2 / 0.05)
        pulse1 = ParametricFunction(lambda t: [t, pulse_func(t), 0], t_range=[-0.5, 0.5], color="#00FFFF")
        pulse2 = ParametricFunction(lambda t: [t, pulse_func(t), 0], t_range=[-0.5, 0.5], color="#00FFFF")
        
        self.place_at_grid(pulse1, "D4", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.place_at_grid(pulse2, "D4", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(hyperbolic_label), Create(pulse1), Create(pulse2))
        self.play(
            pulse1.animate.shift(LEFT * 1.2),
            pulse2.animate.shift(RIGHT * 1.2),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # This classification helps us choose the right solving strategy.
        # Display 'Fundamental Physics' (#FFFFFF) below the three examples.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)
        fundamental_physics = Text("Fundamental Physics", font_size=28, color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(fundamental_physics, "E2", "E5")
        
        self.play(Write(fundamental_physics))
        self.wait(2)

    def construct(self):
        title_text = "The Heat Equation: Modeling Diffusion"
        lecture_lines = [
            "The heat equation describes how temperature spreads through space.",
            "Time change depends on the curvature of spatial temperature.",
            "High curvature means heat flows quickly into colder regions.",
            "Over time, temperature gradients flatten toward a steady state.",
            "This parabolic behavior models diffusion in many physical systems."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        RECT_COLOR = "#0000FF"

        CURVE_COLOR = "#FF0000"
        ARROW_COLOR = "#FFFFFF"
